title: Perfect, pluperfect and the principal parts

objectives.can: Recognise perfect and pluperfect indicatives, active and middle-passive, and parse them.
Name the tense of any indicative form of a common verb and connect it with its headword.

explanation.summary: The perfect presents a state that results from an action: the thing was done and now stands so. It is marked by reduplication, a repeated first consonant. The principal parts are the handful of forms from which all the tenses of a verb can be recognised, and you need them to find a form's headword.

sections.heading: What the perfect presents
body: The perfect looks at a state that exists as the result of an earlier action. It does not mean the same as the English 'have' plus a participle. Often the English present perfect is a good translation, often it is not. Compare 1 John 4:10, where ἠγαπήκαμεν (perfect) stands beside ἠγάπησεν (aorist): the aorist presents God's love as a whole event, while the perfect, in the negated clause, speaks of our love as an established state.

γέγραπται is the form you will meet most. It is not simply 'it was written': it says that what was written stands written, and it is how the New Testament writers introduce a quotation of Scripture. Translators usually give 'it is written'. In John 19:30 the cry τετέλεσται presents the work as finished and so complete.
Grammarians sometimes find a perfect that seems to refer to a past event only. How often this happens is debated. Read the context before you decide.

sections.heading: Reduplication
body: The mark of the perfect is reduplication: the first consonant of the stem is repeated with ε. From κρίνω comes κέκρικεν, from δίδωμι δέδωκεν, from πιστεύω πεπίστευκεν, from γίνομαι γέγονεν, from γράφω γέγραπται. Verbs that begin with two consonants or with a vowel do not repeat in this way: they take a plain ἐ-, as in ἔγνωκεν, or they lengthen the vowel as in the augment, as in ἠγαπήκαμεν. In a compound the reduplication stands after the prefix: ἀπέσταλκεν.

A few verbs have their own pattern and have to be learned: ἑώρακεν (ὁράω), εἴρηκεν (λέγω), ἐλήλυθεν (ἔρχομαι), ἐγήγερται (ἐγείρω). Reduplication, not the augment, tells you the tense is perfect; the augment belongs to the past tenses of the indicative.

sections.heading: Active and middle-passive
body: The perfect active usually has a κ before the endings: -κα, -κας, -κε(ν), -καμεν, -κατε, -κασιν. This is the κ in πεπίστευκα or ἀπέσταλκα. Some verbs have no κ and use -α directly: γέγονα, ἑόρακα. The perfect middle-passive does not add a κ and has no connecting vowel; it adds the middle-passive endings to the reduplicated stem: -μαι, -σαι, -ται, -μεθα, -σθε, -νται. So κέκριται, δέδοται, γέγραπται. Because middle and passive share one form, the context decides which is meant.

The pluperfect is the perfect's past: a state that held at some past point. It has the endings -ειν, -εις, -ει, -ειμεν, -ειτε, -εισαν in the active (ἐληλύθει, εἰρήκει, ᾔδεισαν), and it often lacks the augment (γεγόνει beside ἐγεγόνει). In John 6:17 the evening had come and Jesus had not yet come to them: the pluperfect ἐληλύθει describes the situation at that point.

sections.heading: οἶδα
body: οἶδα is formally a perfect but means 'I know'. Its pluperfect is used with the sense of a past: ᾔδει, 'he knew'. It has no regular present in New Testament Greek. You will meet its forms constantly: οἶδα, οἶδας, οἶδεν, οἴδαμεν, οἴδατε, οἴδασιν. Learn it as a separate verb. In John 6:6 ᾔδει tells us what Jesus already knew.

sections.heading: The principal parts
body: Handbooks list six forms of each verb as its principal parts: the present, the future, the aorist active, the perfect active, the perfect middle-passive and the aorist passive. They are the forms from which you can recognise every other. Because stems change from one to another, as the last two lessons showed, you meet a form like εἶπεν or εὗρεν or δέδοται and need to know which headword it belongs to.

Handbooks give the first person singular. The table below gives the third person singular instead, because those are the forms the texts hold for these five verbs; every form in it stands in the texts. Learn the pairs by reading them across.

misunderstandings: The perfect is not the English 'have + participle'. It presents a resulting state, and the English past tense or present may translate it better: οἶδα is 'I know', γέγραπται is 'it is written'.
A form with ε- at the front is not necessarily a past tense with an augment. κέκρικεν has ε after a repeated consonant; that is reduplication.
The pluperfect is not the aorist: it describes a state that held at a past time, not the whole event.
The perfect middle-passive has no connecting vowel and no κ. Do not look for either in γέγραπται or κέκριται.

deeper.heading: Why a state, not an event
body: The Greek perfect began as a form describing the subject's condition, not an action. That is why οἶδα, a perfect, came to mean 'I know': it described a state of having perceived. In later Greek the perfect and the aorist come closer together. The New Testament keeps much of the older sense, but how far some of its perfects still describe a state is disputed.

reading.why: The end of the crucifixion scene is full of the perfect: τετέλεσται, μεμαρτύρηκεν and οἶδεν stand beside aorists such as ἔλαβεν, παρέδωκεν and ἐξῆλθεν, and the Scripture quotations make the perfect's sense of a standing state easy to see.
